title: Newton's Law of Gravitation
notes: **Law statement:** every particle in the universe attracts every other particle with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.
**Formula:** $F = G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}$, where $G = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{kg}^2$ is the universal gravitational constant.
**Vector form:** $\vec{F}_{12} = -G\frac{m_1 m_2}{r^2}\hat{r}_{12}$. The negative sign indicates attraction; the force on mass 1 due to mass 2 points toward mass 2.
**Shell theorem:** a uniform spherical shell attracts an external particle as if all its mass were concentrated at its centre. Inside a uniform shell, the net gravitational force is zero.
**Why $G$ is so small:** gravitational force is much weaker than electromagnetic force. Between two protons, gravity is about $10^{-36}$ times weaker than the electric force.
**Dimensional formula of $G$:** $[G] = [M^{-1}L^3T^{-2}]$. Check: $[F] = [G][m^2]/[r^2] = M^{-1}L^3T^{-2} \times M^2 / L^2 = MLT^{-2}$, correct.
**Cavendish experiment (1798):** first measurement of $G$ using a torsion balance. This also gave the first accurate value for Earth's mass ($M = gR^2/G$).
**Newton's third law applies:** $\vec{F}_{12} = -\vec{F}_{21}$. The force masses exert on each other is equal and opposite.
**Gravitation is a central force:** it acts along the line joining the centres of the two masses. This conservation of angular momentum is why planetary orbits are planar.
**Kepler's laws as consequence:** Newton derived Kepler's three laws of planetary motion from his law of gravitation, unifying terrestrial and celestial mechanics.
confusion: Gravity is always attractive — there are no negative masses to repel. Unlike electric charge, which can be positive or negative.
The inverse-square law applies at all distances, but at very small distances (sub-atomic) other forces dominate and gravity becomes negligible.
Shell theorem only applies to uniform spherical shells or solid spheres of uniform density — it does NOT apply to irregular shapes.
The universal constant $G$ is the same everywhere in the universe — it does not depend on the medium, temperature, or composition of the masses.
practice: Calculate the gravitational force between two 1 kg masses separated by 1 m. Compare this with the weight of a 1 g mass on Earth. Solution: $F = G(1)(1)/1^2 = 6.674 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{N}$. Weight of 1 g = $mg = 0.001 \times 9.8 = 0.0098\,\text{N}$. Gravitational force is about $6.8 \times 10^{-9}$ times smaller.

A satellite orbits at height $h = 300\,\text{km}$ above Earth ($R = 6400\,\text{km}$). Find the orbital speed. Solution: $v = \sqrt{GM/r} = \sqrt{gR^2/(R+h)} = \sqrt{9.8 \times (6.4 \times 10^6)^2 / (6.7 \times 10^6)} = 7.73 \times 10^3\,\text{m/s} = 7.73\,\text{km/s}$.

At what height above Earth's surface does gravity reduce to 25% of its surface value? Solution: $g' = g(R/(R+h))^2 = 0.25g \Rightarrow (R/(R+h))^2 = 0.25 \Rightarrow R/(R+h) = 0.5 \Rightarrow R+h = 2R \Rightarrow h = R = 6400\,\text{km}$.

Two spheres of masses $5\,\text{kg}$ and $10\,\text{kg}$ are placed $0.5\,	ext{m}$ apart. Find the gravitational force between them. Solution: $F = G(5)(10)/(0.5)^2 = (6.674 \times 10^{-11})(50)/0.25 = 1.335 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{N}$.
universalFacts: Gravity is universal — it acts between any two masses anywhere in the universe, from apples falling to galaxies orbiting each other.
The gravitational constant $G$ is the same everywhere in the universe and at all times — it is a fundamental constant of nature.
Inside a uniform spherical shell, gravitational force is exactly zero at every point, not just at the centre — this is a consequence of the inverse-square law.
Newton's law of gravitation and Coulomb's law are both inverse-square laws, but gravity is always attractive while electric forces can be attractive or repulsive.
